slides.title: Section 5 · Application — In Practice
slides.notes:
SECTION 5 · APPLICATION — IN PRACTICE
Applying the Four Consequences of Weak Review Discipline

SECTION LEARNING OUTCOMES:
1. Make evidence-based recovery decisions when results depart from expectations.
2. Establish executive decisions and routines that protect sustained review discipline.

HOW THIS SECTION RUNS:
This is group work and Capstone work. For each of the four consequences of weak review discipline, each group:
1. Simulates a potential gap in the performance of individuals, and a potential gap in the organisational conditions of its strategy.
2. Writes a decision point for recovery for each gap: the decision the executive team takes when the gap appears, and who takes it.
In part 5.2 each group tests the WARD check-up it set for its enterprise Key Result in Unit 6: the alert fires, and the group runs the recovery.
The group chooses its scribe for this work. The scribe types what the group agrees, and the entries appear on every member’s page. Each member then selects Agree. When every member has agreed, the record feeds the team’s Capstone Blueprint.

HOW TO OPEN THE SECTION:

1. Say what the section does.
Say: "For each of the four consequences of weak review discipline, your group simulates a potential gap in the performance of individuals and in the organisational conditions of the strategy in your team’s Capstone Blueprint, and sets a decision point for recovery for each. Then your group tests the WARD check-up it set in Unit 6: the alert fires, and you run the recovery."

2. Say how the group works.
Say: "This is group work. Your group agrees each entry and chooses its scribe for this work. The scribe types, and the entries appear on every member’s page."

3. Say where the work goes.
Say: "This is Capstone work. You read your group’s record at the foot of the section and select Agree. When every member has agreed, your record feeds your team’s Capstone Blueprint."

slides.title: 5.1 · Decision points against the four consequences
slides.notes:
5.1 — DECISION POINTS AGAINST THE FOUR CONSEQUENCES (CAPSTONE WORK)

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Recall the four consequences of part 2.1.
Say: "Missed early warning signals. Gradual diffusion of accountability. Loss of organisational learning. Eroded leadership credibility. Each shows in the performance of individuals and in the organisational conditions."

2. Say what the group completes for each consequence.
Say: "Simulate a potential gap in your strategy: one in the performance of individuals and one in the organisational conditions. For each gap, write the decision point for recovery: the decision the executive team takes when the gap appears, and who takes it. Write it as one sentence: If the gap appears, then the recovery decision, taken by whom."

3. Give one example for each consequence.
Early Warning Signals Are Missed: "If a Key Result shows no movement across two monthly reviews, then a recovery plan is presented at the next executive review, taken by the executive accountable for the Key Result."
Gradual Diffusion of Accountability: "If a Key Result has not been discussed in an executive review for a full month, then it goes first on the agenda of the next review, with the individuals delivering it present, taken by the CEO."
Loss of Organisational Learning: "If the same obstacle is reported in two functions in one quarter, then the executive team names the cause and records what it changes in the way the strategy is executed, taken by the CEO."
Erodes Leadership Credibility: "If a strategic priority is announced with no date for its first review, then the date and the evidence to be brought to it are fixed in the same meeting, taken by the CEO."

4. Say how the group completes it.
Say: "Take the four consequences one at a time, each on its own tab. The lesson for each sits above the boxes."

ON THE PORTAL, AFTER THE TEACHING:
Participants work as a group in part 5.1 of their own file. This is Capstone work. The group chooses its scribe for this work. The scribe types what the group agrees, and the entries appear on every member’s page.
For each of the four consequences, each group writes a potential gap in the performance of individuals and in the organisational conditions, and a decision point for recovery for each: the decision the executive team takes when the gap appears, and who takes it.

slides.title: 5.2 · Testing your WARD
slides.notes:
5.2 — TESTING YOUR WARD (CAPSTONE WORK)

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Recall the check-up.
Say: "In Unit 6 your group set the WARD check-up for its enterprise Key Result: the waypoints, the alert, the recovery and the decider. It was set while the Key Result was on track. Today the alert fires."

2. Fire the alert.
Say: "Choose one of your waypoints and write the result your executive team reads at that review, beyond the alert."

3. Run the recovery.
Ask: "What explains the gap in the individuals and in the organisational conditions? Which recovery do you run, who decides, and when do you check the result again?"
Guide the groups to use the evidence in their Contribution Map and the recovery they set in advance.

4. Give the example from the Unit 6 worked example.
Enterprise Key Result: Increase customer enquiries resolved within 48 hours from 65% to 90% by year-end. Waypoint: 80% by the end of June. Alert: more than three percentage points below a waypoint.
The red flag: At the end of June, 74% of enquiries are resolved within 48 hours against the 80% waypoint: six points below, beyond the alert.
Individuals · what explains the gap: Two teams follow up fewer than 85% of outstanding enquiries on time.
Organisational conditions · what explains the gap: System availability fell to 96% in May, and enquiries waited for the system to return.
The recovery: Team leaders review open enquiries with each owner every morning; IT restores availability to 99% within four weeks; the Customer Service Executive decides and checks the result at the end of July.

ON THE PORTAL, AFTER THE TEACHING:
Participants work as a group in part 5.2 of their own file. This is Capstone work. The group’s WARD from Unit 6 is shown on each page; if it is missing, the group selects Bring in from my Unit 6 page.
1. The group writes the red flag: the waypoint and the result that raises the alert.
2. The group states what explains the gap in the performance of individuals and in the organisational conditions.
3. The group states the recovery: what is done, who decides and when the result is checked again.
4. Each participant reads the record and selects Agree.

AFTER THE SESSION:
The record reaches you with each participant’s submission, under the heading of Section 5. The agreed record feeds the Unit 8 boxes of the team’s Capstone Blueprint: the four consequences in 8A to 8D and the WARD test in 8E.
